lead: A servomotor turns an electrical voltage into mechanical motion. The armature circuit has resistance and inductance, and it also produces a back emf proportional to speed. Current creates torque proportional to current. The torque drives a load with inertia and friction. Two equations, one electrical and one mechanical, join at torque and speed. This chapter derives the transfer function from armature voltage to shaft angle. It is used in position control of robot arms, printers, antenna drives and valve actuators. The same model appears in many lab experiments.
prereq: You need: 1.3 for Laplace transfer functions and 1.4 for J and b.

blocks.text: An armature-controlled DC servomotor has a fixed field. The control input is the armature voltage va(t). The armature circuit has resistance R (Ω) and inductance L (H). The current i(t) (A) obeys the voltage equation.
va = R i + L di/dt + Kb ω
blocks.where: va is armature voltage in V; i is armature current in A; R is armature resistance in Ω; L is armature inductance in H; ω is shaft speed in rad/s; Kb is the back-emf constant in V·s/rad.

blocks.text: Back emf: when the rotor turns, the armature cuts magnetic flux and acts as a generator. This back emf Kb ω opposes va. It is not a separate battery; it is a voltage inside the same winding.
The current produces torque. Kt is the torque constant in N·m/A. In SI units, Kt and Kb are often equal numerically when losses are ignored, but they are separate constants in the model.

blocks.where: T is motor torque in N·m; Kt is torque constant in N·m/A; i is armature current in A.

blocks.text: The load has inertia J (kg·m²) and viscous friction b (N·m·s/rad). Newton's law for rotation gives the mechanical equation with zero load torque. The shaft angle θ (rad) satisfies dθ/dt = ω.
J dω/dt + b ω = T,   dθ/dt = ω
blocks.where: J is load inertia in kg·m²; b is viscous friction in N·m·s/rad; ω is shaft speed in rad/s; T is motor torque in N·m; θ is shaft angle in rad.

blocks.text: Use Laplace transforms with zero initial conditions. Write ω(s) = s θ(s). The electrical equation becomes Va(s) = (R + Ls) I(s) + Kb s θ(s). The torque equation gives T(s) = Kt I(s). The mechanical equation becomes (Js + b) s θ(s) = T(s).

items: From the mechanical side, write I(s) = (Js + b) s θ(s) / Kt.
Substitute this I(s) into the electrical equation.
Multiply both sides by Kt and collect the θ(s) terms.
Divide to get the transfer function.

blocks.text: θ(s)/Va(s) = Kt / {s[(Ls + R)(Js + b) + Kt Kb]}
blocks.where: θ(s) is shaft angle in rad; Va(s) is armature voltage in V; Kt is torque constant in N·m/A; Kb is back-emf constant in V·s/rad; R is armature resistance in Ω; L is armature inductance in H; J is inertia in kg·m²; b is viscous friction in N·m·s/rad.

blocks.text: If the output is speed, the transfer function is ω(s)/Va(s) = Kt / [(Ls + R)(Js + b) + Kt Kb]. The angle transfer has one extra s because θ′ = ω. That extra s is an integrator. The denominator is cubic: one s from angle integration and a second-order electrical-mechanical part after it.

A two-phase AC servomotor has a reference winding and a control winding. The control voltage sets the torque direction and size. It has low rotor inertia, so it starts and stops quickly. Detailed AC servo models need rotating-field theory; only a few universities teach that depth. Most first courses stay with the DC armature model above.

A position control loop uses this motor as the actuator. A command angle θr is compared with the measured angle θ. The error drives an amplifier, and the amplifier output is va. The motor transfer function gives θ(s)/Va(s). The sensor gain sits in the feedback path. Block diagram reduction (see 1.8) then gives the closed-loop transfer function. The same model explains why a printer head or robot joint settles slowly when J and b are large.

Some syllabi call this actuator modelling. The aim is one transfer function from voltage to motion. Speed control uses ω(s)/Va(s); position control uses θ(s)/Va(s). The difference is one factor s, so always check which output the question asks for.

figure.caption: Armature voltage Va is compared with back emf Kb sθ; the difference drives the armature, torque Kt i drives the load, and 1/s turns speed into angle θ. The feedback path carries the back-emf term.

spec.aria: A DC servomotor block diagram: armature voltage drives torque, the load gives speed, 1/s gives angle θ, and Kb s feeds back back-emf.

examples.question: An armature-controlled DC servomotor has R = 1 Ω, L = 0.1 H, Kt = 0.5 N·m/A, Kb = 0.5 V·s/rad, J = 0.01 kg·m² and b = 0.1 N·m·s/rad. The load torque is zero. Find θ(s)/Va(s).
steps: Write the electrical equation in Laplace form: Va(s) = (Ls + R)I(s) + Kb sθ(s). Insert L = 0.1 H and R = 1 Ω: Va = (0.1s + 1)I + 0.5sθ.
Write the mechanical equation: (Js + b)sθ(s) = Kt I(s). Insert J = 0.01 kg·m², b = 0.1 N·m·s/rad and Kt = 0.5 N·m/A: (0.01s + 0.1)sθ = 0.5I.
Use the derived form. The bracket is (Ls + R)(Js + b) + Kt Kb. Compute (0.1s + 1)(0.01s + 0.1) = 0.001s² + 0.02s + 0.1. Add Kt Kb = (0.5)(0.5) = 0.25. The bracket becomes 0.001s² + 0.02s + 0.35.
Multiply the bracket by s and put Kt = 0.5 on top: θ(s)/Va(s) = 0.5/[s(0.001s² + 0.02s + 0.35)] = 0.5/(0.001s³ + 0.02s² + 0.35s).
examples.check:
R = 1.0
L = 0.1
Kt = 0.5
Kb = 0.5
J = 0.01
b = 0.1
a = L * J
c = L * b + R * J
d = R * b + Kt * Kb
print(round(Kt, 6))
print(round(a, 6))
print(round(c, 6))
print(round(d, 6))

traps: Forgetting the back-emf term Kb sθ(s) in the Laplace electrical equation. This term is the feedback from speed to the armature circuit.
Using ω(s) when the question asks for θ(s). Angle adds one factor 1/s because ω = sθ.
Mixing units: Kb is in V·s/rad, not V/rad; Kt is in N·m/A, not N/A.
Cancelling Kt and Kb blindly. They are often equal numerically in SI when losses are ignored, but use the given values.
Adding a load torque when the question says zero load torque. With load torque TL, the mechanical equation becomes J dω/dt + bω = T − TL.

quiz.q: Write the armature voltage equation of a DC servomotor and define Kb.
quiz.a: va = R i + L di/dt + Kb ω. Kb is the back-emf constant in V·s/rad; Kb ω is the voltage generated by rotation.

quiz.q: Why does back emf appear in the armature circuit? How does it affect current when speed rises?
quiz.a: The turning armature acts as a generator, so it produces Kb ω opposing va. For fixed va, a higher speed raises this opposing voltage, so current and torque fall.

quiz.q: A motor has Kt = 0.8 N·m/A and armature current 2.5 A. Find the torque.
For R = 2 Ω, L = 0.05 H, Kt = 0.4 N·m/A, Kb = 0.4 V·s/rad, J = 0.02 kg·m² and b = 0.2 N·m·s/rad, write θ(s)/Va(s) with zero load torque.
A student writes θ(s)/Va(s) = Kt/[(Ls + R)(Js + b) + KtKb]. What is wrong, and what is the correct denominator?
quiz.a: The factor s from θ′ = ω is missing. The correct denominator is s[(Ls + R)(Js + b) + KtKb].

quiz.q: If load torque TL is not zero, where does it enter the model? How does it change the block diagram?
quiz.a: The mechanical equation becomes J dω/dt + bω = T − TL. TL acts as a disturbance torque subtracted before the load block, so it adds a second input to the load summing point.

quiz.q: Why can Kt and Kb be numerically equal in SI units but still be separate constants?
quiz.a: Kt relates current to torque; Kb relates speed to back emf. Energy conversion makes them equal numerically when losses are ignored, but they describe different effects and can be given different values.

quiz.q: A motor has R = 1 Ω, Kt = 0.5 N·m/A, Kb = 0.5 V·s/rad and b = 0.1 N·m·s/rad. With zero load torque and constant va = 10 V, find the steady-state speed.
quiz.a: At steady state, Va = R I + Kbω and KtI = bω. So I = 0.1ω/0.5 = 0.2ω. Then 10 = 1(0.2ω) + 0.5ω = 0.7ω. ω = 14.29 rad/s.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial servo drives add a current loop inside the speed loop and a position loop outside it. The same motor equations appear in CNC machines, robot joints, camera gimbals and electric vehicle traction. Research versions include field-oriented control for AC servomotors, sensorless speed estimation and thermal limiting. The state-variable form of this motor is in Unit 6, State Space Analysis. Search for DC motor transfer function, servo drive cascade control and back-emf constant.
